title: First Interview
description:
A job posting led to this.

A small office in Mapo-gu. Third floor. No elevator.
The sign reads 'Mirae Industrial Tech' — nothing comes up when you search for them.

The interviewer was a woman in her early forties. She picked up the résumé, adjusted her glasses, and read slowly.
The AC hummed loudly. A motorcycle passed outside.

'There's a six-year gap here.'

She set the résumé down and looked at {name}.
'What were you doing?'

Can't say 'paying off debt.' Six years, from twenty-seven to thirty-three, covering for a father who co-signed the wrong loan.
How do you put six years into one sentence.

{name}'s palms were sweating.

choices.text: Tell the truth — 'There were family circumstances.'
choices.result_text:
The interviewer looked at {name} for a moment. Didn't probe further.
Something in her eyes — understanding. Or resignation.
'...I see. You seem like someone who works hard.'

Walking down the stairs, {name} thought:
Whether it leads to a job or not — that was the truth.
And that was the only pride {name} had left right now.

choices.text: Gloss over it — 'I was preparing to start a business.'
choices.result_text:
Packaged it plausibly. The interviewer nodded — but wrote something long in her notes.
Like someone writing 'needs verification.'

Walking down the stairs, {name} thought:
One lie calls for another.
And that weight tends to arrive sooner than expected.

description_orthodox:
A message from a job app. Mapo-gu. Third floor. No elevator.

Counted the stairs on the way up. 29. {name} counts things like this — turning it into numbers makes it lighter.

The interviewer picked up the résumé. Her eyes stopped at the six-year gap.

{name} knew this question was coming. He'd prepared.
Preparing doesn't make it hurt less.
description_unorthodox:
A message from a job app. Mapo-gu. Third floor. No elevator.

'Mirae Industrial Tech.' Funny. If this is the future, the future's pretty narrow.
Doesn't matter. He needs money now, and this whole thing is temporary anyway.

The interviewer flagged the six-year gap. {name} knew that look — 'an odd one.'
Fine. So what if I'm odd.

title: The Number
description:
Goshiwon room. 3 AM. {name} couldn't sleep.

Opened the calculator on the phone.

Minimum wage. Not even 2 million won for a full month of work.
Three billion won ÷ 2 million won = 1,500 months = 125 years.

125 years.

{name} stared at the screen. Laughed, because it was absurd.
Salary alone — mathematically impossible. From the beginning.

Then the phone rang.
Father. At 3 AM.

{name} didn't pick up. Not while staring at this number — there was no way to keep his voice steady.

choices.text: Keep searching job apps after the shift. Seed money first. [Saver mindset]
choices.result_text:
Big money starts from small money.
Even after work, {name} kept scanning job apps. Side work, temp work, two jobs.

Seed money. That's the first gate.
The number 125 years kept drifting in front of the eyes.

choices.text: Go to the library after work. Start studying investing. [Investor mindset]
choices.result_text:
YouTube, books, finance forums.
After work, {name} went to the library.

If salary won't work, money has to work instead.
Compound interest. Leverage. Assets. {name} read those words seriously for the first time.

choices.text: Write business ideas in the notebook. [Founder mindset]
choices.result_text:
{name} wrote something in a notebook.
Gaps. Demand. Supply. What nobody else was doing.

Ideas alone are nothing yet.
But people who write nothing down never begin.

description_orthodox:
Goshiwon. 3 AM.

Couldn't sleep. Opened the calculator on the phone.

Wage 10,000 won/hour. Two million won a month. Gangnam, 3 billion won. 125 years.

{name} wrote down more numbers. Save 3 million won a month. 15% annual return. Compounding.
What looks impossible to the gut, broken into numbers, starts to show a path.
Then the phone rang. Father. At 3 AM.

He didn't pick up. The clearer the path got, the less he knew where to even begin.
description_unorthodox:
Goshiwon. 3 AM.

Couldn't sleep. Opened the calculator on the phone.

Wage 10,000 won/hour. 125 years.

{name} shut the calculator off. This way won't work.
He'd known that from the start. So he needed another way — a different axis than time.
He had to see what others didn't.

Then the phone rang. Father. At 3 AM.

He didn't pick up. The more set he was on finding another road, the heavier that voice felt.
description_low_mental:
Goshiwon. 3 AM.

Couldn't sleep again.

Opened the calculator, then closed it. The number — 125 years — stayed in front of his eyes. Even doing nothing.

His body felt heavy. The air in this room felt heavy.

The phone rang. Father. {name} thought for a moment about whether to answer.

title: 2 AM
description:
2 AM. The goshiwon room. Can't sleep.

Staring at the ceiling, {name} opened Instagram out of habit. Fingers scrolling the feed.

High school friend Park Minho — 'Finally my own home 🏠 Housing lottery win T_T Waited 10 years #allIn #30sHomeowner'
University classmate Lee Suhyeon — Honeymoon photos. Maldives. Turquoise water. A wedding dress.
Department senior Kim Junghoon — Foreign car key flex. BMW 3 Series. 'First day in the company lot 🔑'

Everyone had arrived somewhere.
Only {name} was still at the starting line. No, behind the starting line.

650,000 won rent. Bank balance. The stain on the goshiwon wall.

The hand holding the phone grew heavy.

choices.text: Delete the app — comparison is poison.
choices.result_text:
Held it down. Deleted it.
Watching someone else's finish line won't move {name}'s starting line.

The screen cleared a little. The mind — just a little.
But that empty space felt like it could be filled with something.

choices.text: Use that feeling as fuel — just you wait.
choices.result_text:
Envy turned to anger.
'Just you wait' is dangerous — it can burn the person who feels it.

But right now this is all there is to run on.
{name} turned off the phone and closed the eyes. Seoul's night wasn't over yet.

choices.text: Just look. Jealous is jealous.
choices.result_text:
Scrolled to the end. Even hit Like.

Decided not to pretend not to be jealous. That's honest too.
But the honesty of that night — ached a little long.

description_orthodox:
2 AM. The goshiwon room.

Opened Instagram. Scrolling the feed, {name} stopped.

Park Minho, housing-lottery win. Lee Suhyeon, Maldives honeymoon. Kim Junghoon, foreign car.

{name} worked out how old each was, when they must have started.
Where am I right now?

He knows comparison doesn't help. But without coordinates, you don't know which way you're facing.
description_unorthodox:
2 AM. The goshiwon room.

Opened Instagram. Other people's lives slid past like ads.

Lottery win. Maldives. BMW.

{name} thought — is that it? Is that 'arrival'?
A housing-lottery win is the start of a 30-year mortgage, and after the honeymoon photos, what comes next?

Everyone posts like they've arrived at something. {name} found that a little funny.
About himself, and about them too.
description_long_gosiwon:
2 AM.

Opened Instagram again. Seventh month in this room.

Park Minho, housing-lottery win. Lee Suhyeon, newlywed. Kim Junghoon, foreign car.

{name} set the phone down. Not envy, not anger — just distant.
Some days your own life doesn't feel like your own.
Today was one of those days.

description_if_known.lent_account:
2 AM. The goshiwon room.

Staring at the ceiling, {name}'s fingers found the phone. Instagram.

Park Minho — 'Finally my own home 🏠 Housing lottery win T_T Waited 10 years'
Lee Suhyeon — Maldives honeymoon. Turquoise water. A wedding dress.
Kim Junghoon — BMW 3 Series key flex.

{name} scrolled, then stopped. Does that money have an origin too? The lottery deposit, the wedding budget, the car installments — all of it came from somewhere and flowed somewhere.

The thought circled back to his own account. Two million won landed last week. It would leave again soon. The money passing through that account right now — under whose name is it flowing?

650,000 won rent. Third month in this room. Between the people on the screen and {name}, there was now one more line, and it could not be seen.
description_if_known.kept_clean_hands:
2 AM. The goshiwon room.

Staring at the ceiling, {name}'s fingers found the phone. Instagram.

Park Minho — 'Finally my own home 🏠 Housing lottery win T_T Waited 10 years'
Lee Suhyeon — Maldives honeymoon. Turquoise water. A wedding dress.
Kim Junghoon — BMW 3 Series key flex.

The feed was the same. Everyone had arrived somewhere.

{name} thought of his own account. Two million won could have landed last week. Since the night he blocked the number, the balance had stayed exactly where it was. Exactly there.

650,000 won rent. Third month in this room. What clean hands were worth — {name} counted it out for the first time today.

title: Next Door
description:
Hallway outside the goshiwon shared kitchen. 1 AM.

A narrow corridor with only one fluorescent tube working.
{name} was carrying cup ramyeon back to the room when the door next to his opened.

The neighbor from next door. They'd crossed paths before — but this was the first time.
'...You're doing ramyeon too, hyung.'

He spoke first. Hollows under his eyes. The face of someone who sits for a long time.
Looks about twenty-six. A worn civil service exam book was tucked under his arm.

'Fourth year studying for the civil service exam. This is my last year — I say that every year.'
He gave a half-laugh. A smile that didn't quite reach the eyes.

'What about you, hyung? What do you do?'

choices.text: 'I don't really know yet. Still figuring it out.'
choices.result_text:
Hyunsu nodded.
'That's the most honest answer.'

The two of them ate ramyeon in silence in the narrow hallway.
Just knowing there's someone on the other side of this thin wall in the same situation —
tonight was a little less cold.

choices.text: 'I'm going to Gangnam. Within five years.'
choices.result_text:
Hyunsu stopped mid-ramyeon and looked at {name}.
Expected a laugh. Didn't get one.
'...You mean it, don't you, hyung.'

A short silence. Then, quietly:
'Somehow I feel like you'll actually go.'
That line stayed. Coming from someone who'd been looking at the same wall for four years.

description_orthodox:
Hallway outside the goshiwon shared kitchen. 1 AM.

As {name} turned to head back with his cup ramyeon, the man next door came out.

"You're on ramyeon too, hyung."

Grade 9 civil service exam prep book. Worn cover. Four years, easy.

This path is a path too. The sure, slow one.
{name} briefly measured the road he'd chosen against this man's.
description_unorthodox:
Hallway outside the goshiwon shared kitchen. 1 AM.

The man next door came out. Grade 9 civil service exam prep book.

"You're on ramyeon too, hyung."

{name} thought — what does he see, studying that every single day?
If he passes, where does he go? On 2.2 million won a month, can he even get out of this goshiwon?
He didn't ask. Everyone has their own math.

title: Two Months In
description:
2 AM.

The ramyeon broth had gone cold.
After Hyunsu went back inside, {name} stood in the hallway alone for a while.

His first two months in Seoul — the burner account text, his father's call, the first Gangnam cafe he ever walked into, Hyunsu's ramyeon.

Back in the room, {name} opens the notebook. First line:
'3 billion won. Five years.'

Nothing below it.

Under fluorescent light: a 4.5-pyeong goshiwon room. One desk. One blanket.
Can 3 billion won actually come out of here?

{name} still doesn't have an answer.
But — tonight was the first time the question felt completely real.

choices.text: Close the notebook. That's enough for today.
choices.result_text:
Turned off the light.

In the dark, the number 3 billion won remained.
The distance between that number and this room — that's exactly the distance ahead.

{name} closed his eyes. No plan yet. Still — he thought he could sleep tonight.

choices.text: Write one more line: 'Wake up at 7 AM tomorrow.'
choices.result_text:
7 AM tomorrow. Below that first line — 3 billion won with nothing under it — just that.

Three billion won is far. 7 AM is close.
He decided to start with the smallest thing he could actually do right now.

Turned off the light. {name} thought tomorrow might be just a little different from today.

title: Why Gangnam?
description:
A small real estate office in the Sinchon alleys.
Walked in to check studio apartment prices.

A man in his fifties looked at {name} over his glasses.
'A studio? With your budget, the deposit's going to be tight.'

True — nothing to say to that. About to leave when he called.
'Have a coffee before you go. No customers anyway.'

He made instant coffee, then asked:
'Where do you want to live?'
'...Gangnam.'
He didn't smile or sneer. Just looked.
'Why?'

choices.text: 'I... want to show my father. Just once.'
choices.result_text:
The first time that reason had been spoken out loud.
"Where are you from?" Sangchul asked.
"Changwon."
The hand stirring his coffee stopped — just for half a beat.
Then he looked at {name} for a long moment, and nodded.
"That 'why' is solid. Then that's enough."
"When you're shaken, it'll hold you. Here's my card — stop by sometime."
For the first time in an unfamiliar city — {name} had someone to know.

choices.text: 'Doesn't everyone want Gangnam if they have the money?'
choices.result_text:
Im Sangchul chuckled.
'Never seen someone who answered that way actually make it.'
'If Gangnam is the goal, you won't get there. Only people who use Gangnam as a means do.'
Didn't know what that meant then. Left with just the business card.

choices.text: Honest — 'Because I refuse to lose. To this city.'
choices.result_text:
Im Sangchul set down his coffee.
'...I said the same thing thirty years ago. Coming up from South Chungcheong Province.'
'That stubbornness got me this far. Two buildings. But I also lost a lot.'
'You — don't lose anything. If you're going, go without losing.'
There was a weight in that.

description_orthodox:
A small real estate office in the Sinchon alleys.

Deposit-to-rent ratio. Still doesn't add up.

The man behind the desk seemed to read {name}'s math.
"With your situation right now, it'll be tough."

How did he know? Or maybe everyone walks in wearing this same look.

"Have a cup of coffee before you go." {name} sat down.
Something told him there was something to learn from this man.
description_unorthodox:
A small real estate office in the Sinchon alleys.

Asked the going rate for a studio. Still a long way off.

"With your situation right now, it'll be tough." A man in his fifties. Blunt way of talking.

{name} looked at him a moment. This guy knows something — just a feeling.
Thirty years in Seoul teaches you a few things. Some of them are worth more than money.
He took the coffee.

title: Contact
description:
Spring afternoon. On the way to work.
Pedaling the bike, turning into an alley — a black sedan swung out and clipped the front wheel.

{name} hit the asphalt. Knee scraped. Front wheel bent.

A woman steps out from the driver's seat. Early thirties. Long black hair, a cream tailored suit, and a composure that looks more expensive than the car. But right now, she is clearly shaken.

'Oh no — are you okay? I can call insurance—'

{name} stands the bike back up. Checks the wheel. Checks the watch.
40 minutes to the start of the shift.

choices.text: 'I'm fine.' — Just leave.
choices.result_text:
No compensation, no contact. {name} walks.
Doesn't look back.

The woman stays rooted to the spot, watching the figure recede.
— Never seen anyone do that before.

choices.text: Show the bent wheel — 'Just the repair cost, please.'
choices.result_text:
She takes out two 50,000 won notes from her wallet. No hesitation.
'Is that enough? If not—'
'It's fine.'

{name} pockets the money and walks.
To her, this was probably lunch money.

choices.text: Get angry — 'You need to watch where you're driving.'
choices.result_text:
Words that had been held in came out. She bows her head.
'...I'm really sorry.'

It seemed genuine. Which made it impossible to stay angry.
{name} sighs and walks the bent bike away.
The weight of her gaze lingered.

description_orthodox:
Spring afternoon. A Sinchon back road.

A black sedan came around the corner and clipped the bike. He went down. Knee bleeding. Wheel bent.

The car door opened. A woman in her early thirties. A flustered look.

{name} tallied the losses — wheel repair, the late penalty at work, hospital fees.

"The hospital's fine. Just the repair—"

Then he checked his watch. 40 minutes until his shift. No time to argue now.
description_unorthodox:
Spring afternoon. A Sinchon back road.

Black sedan. Corner. Impact. Down.

Getting up, {name} caught the plate. Foreign car. Money in this neighborhood.

The woman stepped out. Playing flustered, but her eyes were calm. Someone used to situations like this.

"You should really see a doctor—"

{name} worked out that he had 40 minutes until his shift.
And that this woman owed something.

title: You Again
description:
Convenience store night shift.
Past midnight. The door chime rings.

{name} stops.
It's her. The woman who drove the car that hit the bike.

She recognizes {name} too. Her eyes go wide.
'...Oh? The one from—?'

A bottle of wine in her hand. Clothes that don't belong in this neighborhood.
Why is she here, at this hour, at this store?

choices.text: Pretend not to know her. Ring it up.
choices.result_text:
'15,000 won.'
{name} scans the barcode mechanically.

She looks like she's about to say something. Hands over the card. Bags up. Picks it up.
At the door, one last look back.
'...You work here.'
The door closes. Chime rings.

choices.text: 'The car.' Acknowledge her first.
choices.result_text:
Her face lights up. Relieved.
'You remember me! I felt so bad — I looked around for a while after you left.'
'Nothing to look for.'
'But people don't usually just walk away like that.'
She hesitates a moment, then:
'I'm Han Jiyeon.'
For the first time that day — a name.

title: Let Me Make It Up to You
description:
A few days later. Coming out after my shift, that car is parked in front of the convenience store.

Han Jiyeon steps out. This time it looks like she came determined.

"Just let me buy you one coffee. If not that, then a meal.
It's been weighing on me. That day was my fault, and you walked away without taking anything."

She seems to mean it.

choices.text: Decline — "Don't worry about it. I'm really fine."
choices.result_text:
{name} shakes his head and walks toward the subway station.

Jiyeon doesn't follow. Instead, she calls out behind him.
"Why do you keep running away?"

{name} doesn't stop. But the words keep following him.
— Running? Is this running away?
That day, Jiyeon grew more curious about the person called {name}.

choices.text: Accept the coffee — just once
choices.result_text:
They sat across from each other at a cafe. She had a 6,500 won latte; {name}, the cheapest americano.

Jiyeon talked a lot. About studying abroad, her father's company, her stifling family.
{name} mostly just listened.

"And you? What do you do?"
"...A bit of this and that."
She didn't press further. She just smiled.
"Let's meet again. Next time you're buying, not me."
As if there would be a next time.

choices.text: Be honest — "The worlds we live in are too different."
choices.result_text:
For the first time, {name} spoke honestly.
"Do you know how many months of my rent your car is worth? Buying one coffee is nothing to you, but to me it isn't."

Jiyeon was quiet for a while.
"...So that's why you just left that day?"
"Yes."
"But you know what." She looked {name} straight in the eye.
"I've never met someone like that. Which makes me want to know you more."
That look shook {name}.

title: Her World
description:
Jiyeon said she was buying lunch. A promise.

She took {name} to a Korean restaurant in Cheongdam. Lunch set: 40,000 won.

{name} opened the menu, closed it, opened it again, closed it.

She pretended not to notice. Or really didn't.
After ordering she said:

'Actually you're interested in investing. You're studying for your father's company, but there's no one in your circle who does this, which is frustrating.'

{name} thought for a moment.
What exactly does this person want — impossible to read clearly.

choices.text: 'I'm studying it too. Let's talk.' — Approach as investment partners.
choices.result_text:
Two hours of real estate, pre-sales, investment talk.
Jiyeon knew a lot. Had studied hard.
What {name} knew and what she knew were different. Because of where they came from.
{name} tried to pay for the lunch. Reached — but she'd already put down the card.

choices.text: 'Let's just enjoy lunch today.' — Don't define the relationship yet.
choices.result_text:
Lunch was good. Conversation light.
On the way out she said: 'Where do you want to go next time?'
'Next time' was created. What kind of next time — still unknown.

title: After
description:
The morning after {name} told her everything —
Jiyeon sent a message first.

'you're scared you might still be angry.
You talked so much yesterday... You're a little weird, aren't you?'

{name} stared at the phone.

A woman with three layers of reason.
Because of her father's company. Because she needed an investor. And because she wanted someone close.

What can this become?

choices.text: 'You're not weird. That's just being human.' — Accept it.
choices.result_text:
Sent the reply.
A moment later, hers: 'You're weird too. That's why you like it.'
{name} half-smiled. Felt like there was one more reason to reach Gangnam.

choices.text: 'Jiyeon — Gangnam still comes first for me.' — Draw a clear line.
choices.result_text:
Jiyeon went quiet, then: '...you understand. That's more honest.'
The next day, a document on pre-sale rights came from her.
'If you need help on this side, reach out. That part was genuine.'
Business partners — without the feelings.

choices.text: 'I understand all three reasons.' — No judgment.
choices.result_text:
Jiyeon went quiet a moment, then said: '...That's the scariest thing you've said. Because you're grateful.'
Gangnam and feelings and calculation all tangled in this.
Decided not to give up on it for being complicated.

title: Ten Years
description:
One KakaoTalk message.
"Hey {name}! It's Jaehyuk. Choi Jaehyuk from the army. Remember? I'm in Seoul — let's grab a drink."

Profile picture: him in front of a foreign car.
22 years old. Same barracks. Inseparable through our whole service, then nothing after discharge.

The Jaehyuk at the pojangmacha was different.
Good clothes. Expensive watch. Confidence in every word.
"You haven't changed at all! Let's drink."

choices.text: Glad to see him — an old friend after a long time.
choices.result_text:
Old army stories stretched into the night.
First time laughing out loud in a while. A welcome face in a hard stretch.
'Let's meet up often, {name}. You'll be in touch.'
Jaehyuk seemed genuine. At least that night.

choices.text: Glad, but keeping some distance.
choices.result_text:
Clinked glasses and smiled — but something sat uneasily.
Someone who contacts you after ten years is doing this well.
Why now, why you.
{name} pushed that thought away. It's an old friend.

description_orthodox:
KakaoTalk. Choi Jaehyuk. Army.

Ten years.

The Jaehyuk at the pojangmacha used a foreign car as his profile photo.
Good clothes. Expensive watch. The kind of confidence that fills a room.

{name} smiled warmly and quietly calculated.
What had this person been doing for ten years since discharge.
Why this call, why now.
description_unorthodox:
KakaoTalk. Jaehyuk. Ten years.

Foreign car profile. Expensive watch. Paid for three rounds at the pojangmacha.

Maybe he's just a military buddy who did well.
Or maybe he wants something.

{name} accepted the drink. Too early to tell.

title: Brothers
description:
After that, Jaehyuk kept in touch.
Bought meals, bought drinks, sometimes tried to slip money over.

'You're struggling lately, aren't you? Take this, come on, we're not strangers.'
{name} didn't take it. But the gesture felt genuine.

Today: a café. Jaehyuk takes out his phone.
'{name}, honestly I've been making pretty good money investing. Pretty good money.'
Shows the screen. Profit graph. Numbers going sharply up.
'If you're interested I'll fill you in. No pressure.'

choices.text: Show interest — 'How does it work?'
choices.result_text:
Jaehyuk's eyes lit up.
'I knew you'd get it. I'll tell you everything slowly.'
The returns he showed were unrealistically good.
Too good to be good — {name} forgot that then.

choices.text: Thanks, but pass — 'Investing isn't really my thing.'
choices.result_text:
'Ah, I'm not saying do it now. Just saying.'
Jaehyuk laughed and changed subjects.
But that profit graph stayed in the mind.
If it's real... {name} shook the thought off. For now.

choices.text: Those returns are too good — quietly start to wonder.
choices.result_text:
'Jaehyuk — this looks too good. Is this actually real?'
Jaehyuk's expression froze for half a second, then cleared.
'Ha, that's exactly why everyone doubts it and passes. Your call.'
That half-second — {name} didn't miss it.

title: The Offer
description:
Jaehyuk called a meeting. Hotel lounge.

"I'll be straight with you. {name}, this is just for you.
Something big came in. Triple the principal. But the window closes this week."

He leans forward. Voice drops.

"You want Gangnam, right? How long will that take on a salary? At our age, there's no answer in a paycheck.
You trust me, right? We lived and died together in there."

Triple the principal. This week only.
Both sentences landed at the same time.

choices.text: Put in everything — trust Jaehyuk.
choices.result_text:
Cleaned out the account. Nearly everything.
Jaehyuk pats the shoulder. 'Good call. You'll be laughing soon.'

That night, {name} couldn't sleep.
Whether it was anticipation or dread — impossible to tell.

choices.text: Put in a portion — want in, but won't bet it all.
choices.result_text:
'Jaehyuk, this much is all I can do. More would be too much.'
Jaehyuk looks faintly disappointed. 'Well... still something. Thanks.'
Not going all-in was an instinct.
That instinct might save {name} later.

choices.text: Refuse. And quietly start looking into it.
choices.result_text:
'Let me think about it.' {name} left.
Went home and started searching.
The investment product Jaehyuk mentioned. The company name. Similar fraud cases.

Results started appearing one by one.
A cold feeling ran down the spine.

description_orthodox:
Hotel lounge. Jaehyuk's expression turned serious.

Triple the principal. This week only.

{name} analyzed the structure of those two sentences.
If 'triple' is the hook, 'this week only' is the device that kills thinking time.
Textbook pattern.

Jaehyuk said: "We lived and died together in there."

Because that sentence was true — knowing he should be more careful — {name} wavered anyway.
description_unorthodox:
Hotel lounge. Jaehyuk leaned across the table.

'Triple the principal.'

Every approach {name} had tried — stocks, investment, racetrack — none of them came close to that number.

'This week only.'

The pressure feeling. Not sure if Jaehyuk created it or {name} did.
"We lived and died together in there."

That line was the trigger.

title: No Answer
description:
Settlement day. {name} reached out to Jaehyuk.

choices.text: "Thank you for telling me. But — what if you'd been honest from the start?"
choices.result_text:
Jiyeon lowered her head.
"...You're right. I should have said it from the beginning."
Honesty that came too late. Courage that came too late.
{name} had already known, but hearing it directly was another thing entirely.

choices.text: "That's just how people are. Your world had its own ways."
choices.result_text:
"You... already knew."
For the first time, Jiyeon's face had set down its defenses.
"And you can still say that?"
He'd thought a betrayal you saw coming would hurt less — it didn't, not quite.
Still, forgiveness was also a thing he did for himself.

title: The Rejection Email
description:
A mail notification popped up on his phone.

[Hiring Result] To Mr. Kim Minjun, applicant for the Management Support Team at Daehan Distribution Co., Ltd.

Hello. Thank you for your application.
After reviewing your submission, we regret to inform you that
we are unable to select you in this round of hiring.
We wish you the best in your future endeavors.

{name} closed the phone. Then he looked out the window for a while.

He consoled himself that it was the first rejection — but in truth it was the third.
When there's nothing to put on a résumé, you'd at least like a reason. They don't give that either.

choices.text: It's fine, look for the next posting
choices.result_text:
He opened the job app again. Similar postings, similar requirements, similar feel.
Hitting the apply button was a 0.3-second act of courage.
They usually reply about three weeks later — or never at all.

choices.text: Work on the résumé (revise the cover letter)
choices.result_text:
He opened the cover-letter file. He wrestled for an hour with how to fill the six-month gap.
It's not perfect, but it's better than before.
Every one of these lines will land in an interviewer's eyes someday.

title: The Goshiwon Owner's Meddling
description:
He ran into the goshiwon owner — the ajumma — in the hallway.

'Not heading out to work these days, are you, young man?'

It was phrased as a question, but it was a confirmed fact. There's nothing that happens in this building the ajumma doesn't know.

'There's a night shift open at the convenience store my nephew runs. It's not far either. You want it?'

It's no great position. But with his account in its current state, is this the time to be picky?

choices.text: Thank you. I'll start right away — convenience store night shift
choices.result_text:
He started the next day.
The wage is stingy, but now there's money coming in every month.
The gap between zero and one was bigger than he'd thought.
He bought the ajumma a case of drinks.

choices.text: I appreciate the thought. I'm looking for something better
choices.result_text:
The ajumma laughed, 'Sure, when you're young you should aim high.'
Back in his room, he opened the job postings again.
Choices carry responsibility. His account will show that responsibility.

title: What Came After
description:
He saw the name in the news.
Choi Jaehyuk.

Headline: "Pyramid investment fraud ring arrested, 2.3 billion won in damages."

{name} didn't open the article.
Because opening it felt like he already knew.

The choice from back then came to mind.
Whether he'd turned it over to the police, held leverage over him, or schemed the whole thing together —
that choice came back now, along with this news.

{name} looked out the window for a long time.

choices.text: Turning it over to the police was right — this news proves it  [take_high_road path]
choices.result_text:
The evidence {name} submitted contributed to this outcome.
Not getting his money back was still the case.
But an additional 2.3 billion won in damage was stopped.
Gangnam is still far off. Even so, he wasn't ashamed to look in the mirror.

choices.text: Back then I saved only myself — maybe that was the way to Gangnam  [crossed_line path]
choices.result_text:
He closed the article.
Whether what {name} had done stopped some of that 2.3 billion or added to it, there was no telling.
What kind of person he'd become on the road to Gangnam —
a day was coming when he could no longer dodge that question.

choices.text: Read it as a victim — so he got caught in the end after all  [jaehyuk_scammed path]
choices.result_text:
2.3 billion won. {name}'s money is in there somewhere too.
He won't get it all back. He won't know until the trial's over.
But strangely, closing the article, he could breathe a little easier.
That bastard got caught in the end. That's enough. For now.

title: Memory of the Starting Line
description:
Gangnam had drawn close.

Through this whole journey, Daeun had been at his side — or at some point they'd each gone a different way.

That hand sliding a coffee across the convenience-store counter.
The words she'd said: "You did well today too."

Entering the final stretch, he thought of her.
However things had gone — the fact that she was there at the starting line doesn't change.

choices.text: She's still here — at the end of this road too
choices.result_text:
He sent Daeun a text.
"Almost there."
A reply came. "I'm right here."

{name} slipped the phone into his pocket and kept walking.
This Gangnam dream wasn't being run alone. That was the clearest thing right now.

choices.text: We went our separate ways — but she was the beginning
choices.result_text:
Daeun is living her life, in her own way.
{name} made it this far, in his.

Together or not —
the fact that she was at the starting line isn't something that gets erased.

He held onto that as he walked toward the final stretch.

title: Redevelopment Confirmed
description:
When the phone vibrated, Im Sangchul's name appeared on the screen. Before {name} could answer, a government notice arrived as a PDF.

"Minjun. It's confirmed."

Redevelopment district designation. {name} checked the address and seal, then ran the projected value again. More than two and a half times. His palm sweated while his voice stayed strangely calm.

"This is real estate. Slow, but certain." Sangchul laughed over the line. Only a number had changed, yet for the first time {name} felt like a player at the table instead of a spectator.

choices.text: Ask him to let me know if there's another chance
choices.result_text:
"Please tell me when you find another good one."

"Of course. In this business, people are everything." Sangchul laughed and hung up. The ring of an old office phone slipped into the end of the call.

{name} looked at the buildings outside. It was yesterday's Seoul, yet every window seemed to carry a price tag. Gangnam was still far away, but for the first time the road looked almost straight.

choices.text: Use these gains as fuel for the next bet
choices.result_text:
Before replying to the congratulations, {name} opened a calculator. He split the principal from the gains, then tested how much larger the next return could be if he used more credit.

One victory looked like a formula capable of explaining the world. At last, he could see how money went out and returned with more money behind it. The next property's address began to replace the call log on his screen.

title: Redevelopment Falls Through
description:
Sangchul's call connected later than usual. For a while, only the sound of papers turning came through the receiver.

"Minjun. I'm sorry."

The redevelopment designation had been deferred to the next session. In administrative language it was pending; in the language of money it was effectively dead. The return estimate already included the loss.

Sangchul did not say he had been wrong for the first time in thirty years. He offered no excuse and no next deal. In the voice of a man who usually filled every room, only the apology remained.

choices.text: It can't be helped — I knew the risk going in
choices.result_text:
"I made the decision myself."

The words came more easily than expected. They were sincere, and they also kept the entire loss from hardening into someone else's betrayal.

After the call, {name} entered the returned amount in his ledger. The cell labeled "tuition" was painfully large. Renaming the loss did not bring the money back, but it left room for another line below it.

choices.text: Honestly, it feels like a betrayal
choices.result_text:
{name} hung up without answering. Closing the screen did nothing; the red loss remained against the inside of his eyelids.

A sense of betrayal rose before anger. He had known the deal could fail, but had never pictured the person he trusted being wrong.

Sangchul might be blameless. Tonight, that fact offered no comfort. The phone rang again, and {name} let it stop on its own.

title: The Premium
description:
A message arrived from Han Jiyeon: one congratulatory sticker and the confirmed premium. {name} could not close the notification. He counted the digits again.

The information she had offered was now an amount that would appear in his account. For a moment, he seemed to stand inside the world of Gangnam cafes and effortless introductions under his own name.

He should have felt only joy. Instead, gratitude and relief carried the weight of a debt. He had made money, yet it felt as if he had finally returned something long owed to her.

choices.text: "This is thanks to you. I mean it."
choices.result_text:
"This is thanks to you. I mean it."

The read receipt sat alone for a while. Then Jiyeon replied, "I wanted to hear that, oppa. I'm happy it worked out for you too."

{name} looked again at the little sticker. More than the amount bringing him closer to Gangnam, the fact that she had thought of him first remained. He wrote and erased his next reply until the screen dimmed.

choices.text: Now I stand equal to her world
choices.result_text:
{name} sent a brief thank-you, then opened his investment app. As he divided the profit between principal and the next opportunity, Jiyeon's reply slipped beneath newer notifications.

He had passed through a door she opened, but did not want to remain a guest in her world. With enough money, he could build an entrance carrying his own name. On the next plan, only the amount remained.

title: Pre-Sale Cancelled
description:
The cancellation notice arrived first. Beneath its gray sentences, four words stood out: deposit non-refundable. A moment later, Han Jiyeon called in person.

"I'm sorry. I didn't know either. I checked it again and again...."

Her usually steady voice dropped at the end of each sentence. {name} tried to decide whether it was sincere, but the vanished deposit crowded out every other thought.

He stared at a stain on the goshiwon ceiling. It was the night he learned that even the world Jiyeon crossed so easily contained locked doors.

choices.text: "It's all right. This wasn't your fault."
choices.result_text:
"It's all right. This wasn't your fault."

The words came easily, though his hand tightened around the blanket. He did not want her to hear him break, nor did he want to turn the tremor in her voice into something to blame.

After the call, the room looked smaller. Gangnam was farther away and the deposit was still gone. At least the last sentence had been his own choice.

choices.text: "I should never have trusted you."
choices.result_text:
"I should never have trusted you, or any of your people."

{name} hung up before Jiyeon could answer. When she called again, he let it ring. Her glittering world suddenly looked like a thin stage set.

He saved a screenshot of the loss. Jiyeon's name above it no longer resembled an entrance. From that night on, it read like a warning.

title: The Call
description:
The phone rang. Dad.

A short call.
"You doing all right." "Yeah." "You eating." "I am." "Good."
That was all.

Dad's in Changwon. The factory. Worked there his whole life.
He co-signed a loan guarantee that went bad. The other party vanished. The debt was left behind.
{name} paid it off. Six years. Neither of them brings it up.

After hanging up, the room felt quieter.

choices.text: "Yeah. You too?"
choices.result_text:
"Ate."

A long silence. {name} hung up first.
Spent thirty seconds after the call trying to think of what to say.

Why nothing ever comes out during the call.
Maybe because just hearing the voice already says everything.

choices.text: "Yeah. Dad, I think things are going to work out."
choices.result_text:
"...Yeah?"
Dad's voice shifted slightly. In that one short word.

After hanging up, {name} thought:
There's still so much left to show him. And time isn't endless.

choices.text: Just ask how he is and hang up quickly
choices.result_text:
Call duration: 23 seconds.
"How are you." "Fine." "Okay, hang up then."

{name} put the phone down and stared at the ceiling.
Too many things that couldn't fit into 23 seconds.

description_orthodox:
The phone rang. Dad. The usual short call.
"You doing all right." "Yeah." "You eating." "I am." "Good."

After hanging up, {name} thought — next time, I'd like to have something to report.
Even something small. Something that might let Dad breathe a little easier.
There wasn't anything yet.
description_unorthodox:
The phone rang. Dad. The usual short call.
"You doing all right." "Yeah." "You eating." "I am." "Good."

After hanging up, {name} thought — this call has gone the same way for six years.
Something has to change. So Dad can say something different.
That was one more reason he wanted to reach Gangnam.
description_low_mental:
The phone rang. Dad. The usual short call.
"You doing all right." "Yeah." "You eating." "I am." "Good."

{name} hung up.
The room was quiet.

Dad's voice had sounded a little off — or maybe not. He couldn't tell.
He didn't want to check. If he found out right now, he wasn't sure he could carry it.

title: One Message
description:
A KakaoTalk from an unknown number.

"Minjun? This is Mrs. Choi, the neighbor from Changwon.
I got your number from your father.
He seems to be going to the hospital these days.
Not sure if it's serious, but I thought I should let his son know."

{name} read the screen twice.
Called Dad. The line rang. No answer.
Five minutes later a text came.
"I'm fine, don't worry about it."

choices.text: Reply that you'll come down next week
choices.result_text:
Dad didn't reply.
That wasn't a no, and {name} knew it.
Searched for train tickets. KTX Changwon-Jungang, two and a half hours.
Some things come before money — learned that this time.

choices.text: Call to check — can't be that serious
choices.result_text:
Called again. He answered this time.
"I'm fine. Just a regular check-up. Nothing major."
Firm. {name} didn't press further.
Wanted to believe he was fine.
The difference between believing and wanting to believe — couldn't tell them apart yet.

choices.text: Can't afford to go down right now — once things settle
choices.result_text:
Pulled up train tickets. Then closed the tab.
Not yet. A little more money first, then go down.
Just a little more.

How much was "a little" — {name} didn't really know.

description_orthodox:
A KakaoTalk from an unknown number.

"Minjun? This is Mrs. Choi, the neighbor from Changwon. Your father seems to be going to the hospital these days.
Not sure it's serious, but I thought I should let his son know."

{name} ran the schedule right away.
Next day off, the KTX timetable, the work he couldn't skip.
Living a steady life meant factoring even this into the math.

He called his father. No answer.
Five minutes later, a text. "I'm fine, don't worry about it."
description_low_mental:
A KakaoTalk from an unknown number.

"Minjun? This is Mrs. Choi, the neighbor from Changwon. Your father seems to be going to the hospital these days.
Not sure it's serious, but I thought his son should know."

{name} stared at the screen. His head went blank.
Right now he had no strength to worry, none to go down there.
That only turned into more guilt.

He called his father. No answer.
Five minutes later, a text. "I'm fine, don't worry about it."

title: Mom's Call
description:
Mom called. She hadn't been in touch in a long time.

"Minjun."

Just the voice was enough to know.

Dad had collapsed. A cerebrovascular episode. Changwon Sungsim Hospital ER.
Stabilized now. Conscious, talking.

"Should only need a few days in hospital. No surgery.
But going forward he has to be careful.
The doctor said... if he doesn't manage it properly, it could happen again anytime."

{name}'s hands trembled briefly.

choices.text: Go down right now
choices.result_text:
Booked the first KTX to Changwon. 5 a.m. from Seoul Station.
On the train, tried to picture Dad's face.
Started calculating when the last time was —
Stopped. Too long ago.

choices.text: Say you'll go down within the week
choices.result_text:
"I'll come on the weekend."
Mom went quiet for a moment.
"Yeah. I called because I thought your dad would worry a lot."
Something buried under those words.
{name} hung up, then thought about how far away the weekend felt.

choices.text: Send money — too busy with things here
choices.result_text:
Transferred the money. For hospital expenses.
Mom said "Thank you."
Dad would ask whose money it was.
{name} decided not to think about what Mom would say.

choices.text: Called Sangchul — he'd know someone
choices.result_text:
Sangchul picked up and within minutes had connected a doctor he knew near Changwon.
Fast. No questions.
"This is the kind of thing you have to handle," was all he said.

Dad was moved to a better room.
Mom asked what had happened.
{name} just said, "Someone I know helped out."

description_unorthodox:
A call from his mother, who hadn't been in touch in a long time.

"Minjun."

Dad had collapsed. A cerebrovascular warning. Changwon Sungsim Hospital.

{name} thought of the moves he had in play right now.
Investments underway, timing he had to catch, things that would wobble if he stepped away.

And then he hated himself for it.
That with his father down, the money math had spun up first in his head.
description_low_mental:
A call from his mother, who hadn't been in touch in a long time.

"Minjun."

He knew just from her voice.

Dad had collapsed. A cerebrovascular warning. Changwon Sungsim Hospital.
Stable now, they said. Conscious, talking.

{name}'s hands shook. His mind was already at the bottom, and now this landed on top of it.
Telling himself he couldn't fall apart, he felt himself already falling apart.

title: Changwon
description:
Changwon Sungsim Hospital. Room 301.

The hallway smelled of disinfectant. Different air from Seoul.
Asked the nurse for Dad's room number.

Opened the door.
Dad was sitting up in bed, looking out the window.
Changwon sky. Low buildings. Factory smokestacks.

Thin hands. Hands that had gripped factory floors his whole life.
Shoulders more hunched. Hair more white.

{name} paused at the doorway.
Dad turned around without a sound. Eyes met.

A long silence passed.

Dad spoke. "...Minjun."
Then another pause.
"I'm sorry."

choices.text: "It's not your fault, Dad." — first time saying those words
choices.result_text:
The room was quiet.

{name} sat in the chair beside the bed.
Father looked toward the window. Changwon sky. Low buildings.

No words.
"Did you eat?" "I ate." "When do you get out?" "Next week probably." "I see."

This is what father and son conversation looks like.
For six years, while paying off the debt in Seoul, {name} never once asked.
Why he'd signed the guarantee. Whether he regretted it. Whether he'd wanted to say thank you.

{name} thought: I'll ask later.
But how much 'later' is left — no one knows.

choices.text: "When I make it to Gangnam, you're the first person I'll bring."
choices.result_text:
Father said "I'm sorry."

{name} didn't know what to say.
'It's okay' is a lie. Six years of repayment.
'I'm sorry too' doesn't fit. There was nothing to be sorry for.

So he just stayed.

Father's thin hand. Bent shoulders.
The hand that gripped factory floors for a lifetime lay on top of the blanket.

{name} placed his hand over his father's.
Without words.

Outside, the Changwon sun began to set.

choices.text: Can't say anything — just sit beside him
choices.result_text:
There was so much to say, and none of it came out.
Just sat down beside him. Dad didn't speak either.

Two hours like that.
Later, {name} would understand that was the best way.

title: After That
description:
After coming back from Changwon, the calls with Dad changed.

Still not many words.
But now there was something more after "did you eat."

Today Dad called first.
Not Sunday evening. Wednesday afternoon.

"Minjun. How's the weather in Seoul?"

choices.text: "Cold here. Cold there too, right?" — just talk about small things
choices.result_text:
Fifteen minutes of weather, the neighborhood, nothing in particular.

After hanging up, {name} was smiling.

Not a word about Gangnam.
But today that felt better. Because Dad called first.

choices.text: "I'm doing well lately, Dad. Don't worry."
choices.result_text:
Dad's voice sounded warm.

"I'm doing fine too. And so are you."
A brief silence.
"...Yeah. Me too."

That was all. But the feeling after the call was different today.

title: Hey, Actually Me Too...
description:
The second meeting at the pojangmacha went late.

Jaehyuk poured another round of soju.
His eyes were hazier than usual.

"Hey {name}. I... actually, I got burned too, back then."

{name} put down the chopsticks.

"A senior I knew talked to me about an investment. Said it was a great opportunity. You know how rough things were for me at the time. So I put money in. And then..."

Jaehyuk trails off.

"The strange thing is, later that senior asked if I wanted to become one of the operators. Said I'd be good at it. Looking back, it's funny."

He laughs bitterly.

Seems like he's about to say more — takes a sip instead. That's all for tonight.

choices.text: "So what happened?" — listen comfortably
choices.result_text:
Jaehyuk laughed. 'Ah, that's ancient history. Things are fine now, right?'
He changed the subject. {name} didn't push.
But those words kept nagging. So what happened, exactly.

choices.text: "Being an operator... you still doing that now?" — ask directly
choices.result_text:
Jaehyuk's eyes hardened for a moment.
'...What are you talking about. That's all in the past.'
He smiled and offered more to drink.
{name} accepted the glass, and didn't forget that brief flash in his eyes.

title: No-Strings Help
description:
Met at a cafe. Jaehyuk said he had good news.

It wasn't about investments.

"Hey, I know this guy who's an HR team leader at a mid-size company — send him your resume. I already mentioned you."

{name} paused.

"Why are you doing this for me?"

Jaehyuk smiled. "Come on, what are we to each other? You think I forgot how good you were to me in the army? I haven't."

He held out a business card with a contact on it.

Needs thinking through. Is this genuine goodwill — or a way to pull {name} in deeper?

choices.text: "Thanks. You're a real friend." — accept the offer
choices.result_text:
Took the card. Plan to reach out.
Jaehyuk really did have a good side.
What {name} didn't know then — that would make what came later hurt more.

choices.text: "Jaehyuk, honestly — why are you so good to me?" — probe the motive
choices.result_text:
A flash of hurt crossed Jaehyuk's face.
'...You think I'm doing this for something? That hurts.'
{name} hovered somewhere between guilt and suspicion.
Took the card. Never called.

title: Back from Zero
description:
A month since getting scammed.

Sat and calculated the amount lost.
Calculated it again. The number didn't change.

{name} took out a notebook.

What was in the account when first coming to this city?
Almost nothing, back then too. And somehow it worked out.

The difference between now and then —
Meeting someone like Choi Jaehyuk.
And now knowing why those words sounded so sweet.

{name} started writing.

choices.text: Write down what was learned, not what was lost — turn this into money
choices.result_text:
Wrote down everything Jaehyuk had said.
How he'd played on emotions. Which words had made the heart waver.
This was expensive tuition. But if tuition was paid, something had to be learned.
{name} closed the notebook and turned the computer back on.

choices.text: Get up early tomorrow morning — start over from the basics
choices.result_text:
Set the alarm for 6 a.m.
No grand plan. Just: get up in the morning, eat, do something.
That was all. That was where it started.
Thought of Jaehyuk for a moment — then opened the notebook.

description_if_known.jaehyuk_night_was_real:
A month since getting scammed.

The number hadn't changed.

But {name} didn't delete the photo.
The two of them in front of the pojangmacha.
That night was that night.

{name} took out the notebook. Decided to write only what came after that night.
description_if_known.deleted_jaehyuk_photo:
A month since getting scammed.

The number hadn't changed.

{name} deleted the photo too. Deleted the contact.
The pojangmacha, the army stories, the laughter of that night —
erased all of it together.

{name} took out the notebook. Started over from the beginning.

title: Thin Wall
description:
At three in the morning, even the corridor's sensor light had gone dark. With his eyes closed, {name} could distinguish the mini-fridge motor from water moving through the pipes.

Then another sound came through the next room. He first mistook it for a television, but it was someone failing to swallow a sob. The thin plasterboard hid a face without stopping the voice.

{name} looked at the ceiling. In every small room in the building, someone seemed to be awake for a different reason.

choices.text: Put in earplugs — not my business
choices.result_text:
{name} pushed the earplugs in. The crying did not vanish; it moved outside with the hum of the fridge. Soon he could hear only his own muffled heartbeat.

Telling himself it was none of his business might let him sleep. He pulled up the blanket without deciding whether this was self-protection or practice at erasing someone else's pain.

choices.text: Knock once on the wall — asking if they're okay
choices.result_text:
{name} tapped twice with his knuckle. The crying stopped. He asked, "Are you all right?" After a long pause, a very small "Yes" came back.

Both of them probably knew it was not true. He asked nothing more. Between two people who knew neither face nor name, the thin wall felt for once less like a barrier than a connection.

choices.text: Stare at the ceiling too — get through the night together
choices.result_text:
{name} stared at the ceiling without speaking. The sobs weakened, then returned. Unable to sleep, he crossed the same hour beside them.

How many people in this building slept easily? The thought was sad, yet carried a strange warmth. They could not save one another, but at least no one was crossing this night entirely alone.

title: First Day on the App
description:
A brokerage account confirmation appeared on the laptop over the goshiwon desk. After several rounds of identity checks, the first screen looked almost indifferent.

Red and blue candles on the Korean stock chart changed without pause. Whenever one figure moved, someone gained and someone lost. Soon, {name}'s money could enter the same movement.

An admission ticket felt closer than fear. He had not bought anything, yet every flicker on the screen already seemed nearer than before.

choices.text: Put in 10,000 won — have to feel it to understand it
choices.result_text:
{name} deposited 10,000 won and bought one share. When the fill alert sounded, the market price stopped being someone else's number. A rise of a few won lifted his mouth; a fall made him refresh.

It was too little to call a profit. Still, he learned that his body reacted before thought whenever money moved. The first lesson was not the chart, but his own pulse.

choices.text: Read a book first — understand it before going in
choices.result_text:
The account was open, but {name} did not press Deposit. Instead, he searched order types, fees, and examples of losses, filling the first page of a notebook. Every sentence contained another unknown word.

Today's profit was zero. So was the loss. The empty balance no longer looked like proof that he was behind, but like space that would remain until he understood where he was entering.

title: First Line of the Cover Letter
description:
The first cover-letter prompt filled the laptop screen: "Please describe your motivation for applying." A cursor blinked steadily inside the white field.

Thirty-three. No career. A six-year gap. Every opening sentence stopped at those facts. Honesty sounded like an excuse; polishing it too smoothly produced someone else's resume.

The deadline drew nearer while the field stayed empty. {name} had to choose a first sentence somewhere between the applicant the company wanted and the person sitting in this room.

choices.text: Write honestly — explain the gap
choices.result_text:
{name} wrote why he had stopped for six years and why he had returned to Seoul. Reading it back, the gap appeared before any achievement. It still looked bleak.

At least he could answer the same question in an interview without looking away. When he pressed Save, the cursor stopped. His work history was empty, but the first sentence remained in his own voice.

choices.text: Dress it up — make it sound good
choices.result_text:
The gap became a period of self-directed study, and irregular jobs became project experience. None of it was false. The failed days and hours spent motionless in his room simply vanished between sentences.

The finished letter was hard to fault. {name} separately memorized answers for the questions it would invite. Performing the person in the document became part of preparing for the interview.

choices.text: Just submit — speed over perfection
choices.result_text:
Five minutes before the deadline, {name} stopped editing and pressed Submit. An awkward sentence came to mind immediately, but there was no longer a way to change it.

The confirmation email replaced the empty field with an application number. An imperfect document could at least be judged. His tense face and a trace of relief appeared together on the dark laptop screen.

title: Idea Notebook
description:
Lying on the goshiwon bed, {name} opened a notes app. Ideas that had seemed complete before he came to Seoul could not become even one line against the empty screen.

He typed a service name, erased it, then tried to explain why anyone would use it. Kept inside his head, the idea had been possibility. Written down, it showed its holes first.

If he left it unrecorded, tomorrow he would remember it as better than it was. He had to choose between preserving an embarrassing first sentence and waiting for a finer thought.

choices.text: Search it right now — see if it already exists
choices.result_text:
The search results contained several similar services. Their names and features were more concrete than {name}'s note. For a moment, he felt as if someone had stolen an idea he had never shared.

Then the reviews revealed complaints users repeated. The road to being first was closed, but there was still something to repair more precisely. A one-star review became the first line of his new note.

choices.text: Just write everything down — judge later
choices.result_text:
{name} postponed judgment and wrote down everything that came. By dawn, the list held fourteen ideas. Half were absurd; a few were already too vague to understand.

At least the screen was no longer empty. For now, he would not separate possibility from scribble. The cursor blinked after the final number, leaving a place for a fifteenth thought.

title: First Meetup
description:
The finance study group {name} found online met around a long cafe table. People introduced their companies and titles before mentioning what they had ordered.

Business cards landed one by one in front of him. Everyone had a job; when his turn came, he had no paper to offer. He took out his phone, saved each number, and repeated every name twice.

On the subway home, the corners of the cards pressed through his pocket. He could not tell whether he had met people or collected a list of uses they might trade.

choices.text: Saved their contacts — might be useful later
choices.result_text:
{name} added each person's company, interests, and first topic beside their name. He promised himself he would send each of them one relevant article before the next meeting.

Days later, one person replied. A short thank-you ended with a suggestion to meet again next week. The first name in the list no longer looked like an unfamiliar business card.

choices.text: Felt uneasy walking home — what was I trying to get here?
choices.result_text:
As he walked home, {name} asked why he had gone. He wanted useful information, perhaps, but also to sit among people who could name a workplace. The answers overlapped.

Numbers saved without purpose were contacts, not a network. Next time, he would write down one thing he could offer and one thing he needed. The cards in his pocket felt heavier than before.

title: Three Hours of Charts
description:
The goshiwon light was off, and only the laptop lit the desk. Three videos on indicators, moving averages, and trading volume ended one after another.

Lines that had meant nothing seemed slightly more legible. Then the next chart broke the rule he had just learned. Understanding and illusion grew at the same pace.

The taskbar clock had passed two in the morning. One more video seemed likely to connect everything, while tomorrow's body was already asking him to stop tonight.

choices.text: Keep watching — something's about to click
choices.result_text:
{name} played the next video. His notes gained golden crosses and the MACD formula; the clock reached four. Whenever he blinked, the lines on the screen briefly doubled.

Solving the final question produced a clear sensation of learning. Red and blue candles remained after he closed the laptop. He had put tomorrow's concentration into tonight's lesson too.

choices.text: Sleep — fresh mind tomorrow
choices.result_text:
{name} saved the unplayed video and closed the laptop. In the sudden darkness, the mini-fridge sounded louder.

The strength to sit down again tomorrow mattered more than one term memorized tonight. He set his alarm an hour early and lay down. The chart remained unsolved, but he knew exactly where to reopen it.

title: Account Balance
description:
Only after the month-end alert appeared did {name} open his banking app. Goshiwon rent, phone bill, transit card, convenience-store purchases. Small charges stood in rows by date.

Balance: {money}.

He had not lost one large sum. The daily price of existing in Seoul had simply thinned the account piece by piece. In his head it was living expense; on the screen it looked like time remaining. His face hovered in the cold light.

choices.text: Listed out expenses — where can I cut?
choices.result_text:
{name} divided the charges into food, transport, and fixed costs. Only meals could really shrink. A 2,800-won lunch box, twice a day, came to roughly 160,000 won a month.

Once the table was complete, the shapeless fear fit inside cells. It felt absurd to budget even his future hunger. Still, what he would have to endure was clearer than before.

choices.text: Closed the app — check it later
choices.result_text:
{name} swiped the app away. If he did not look, he could live briefly as if the problem did not exist. He knew that was a lie.

His face appeared when the screen went black. The balance vanished, but the rent date kept approaching. He put the phone face down and left his hand on it, waiting for an alert that had never sounded.

choices.text: Looked for part-time work right away
choices.result_text:
Instead of the bank, {name} opened a job app. Convenience-store nights, warehouse loading, gas station. The listed 10,320 won an hour looked more real than his balance.

Eight hours times a month of shifts came to about 2.1 million won. Beside the money he could earn sat the time he would lose. He saved three listings. Tomorrow, he would decide whether to press Apply.

title: Little by Little
description:
{name} opened his banking app to close out the month. Beneath the rent and living costs, deposits remained. For the first time, more had entered than left.

Balance: {money}.

It was too small to show anyone, less than a dot beside three billion won. Still, {name} watched the screen. For the first time since coming to Seoul, his account had not shrunk. The figure seemed to be moving forward, very slowly.

choices.text: Took a screenshot — keeping a record
choices.result_text:
{name} took a screenshot. In his photo library, the small balance settled between receipts and a copy of his ID.

He planned to look again when the amount had grown enough to seem laughable. Even if that day never came, the image proved that today he had not moved backward. The timestamp itself looked worth preserving.

choices.text: Wrote down next month's goal
choices.result_text:
{name} opened his notes and wrote a target balance for next month. It was slightly higher than this month's, reachable if he stretched. Below it, he listed the shifts needed and expenses to cut.

For the first time, the vague future contained a box he could check. One line that could be crossed out. He pinned the note to the top. The next month had not arrived, but its number already had a place.

choices.text: Thought: this is nothing — still so far
choices.result_text:
{name} calculated the percentage of his goal: zero point zero-something. The pleasure of growth became tiny below the decimal. He told himself this was no place to relax.

When he closed the app, the brief curve of his mouth disappeared too. Delaying satisfaction seemed like a way to travel farther. No one was in the room to celebrate, and he left himself nothing to say.

title: This Is Actually Working
description:
After checking the deposit alert, {name} closed his banking app and opened it again.

Balance: {money}.

He had arrived in Seoul with only 500,000 won. Now he traced the figure with one finger and counted its digits three times. It was neither a mistake nor an unsettled payment.

His heart accelerated before joy arrived. He could not separate skill from luck in the money he had made. The brighter the balance looked, the more clearly he could see how much there was to lose.

choices.text: This is luck — don't get carried away
choices.result_text:
After one look at the balance, {name} covered the screen. He knew the next order grew dangerous the moment one lucky break became proof of skill.

He wrote down each source of profit and labeled what he could not reproduce as luck. Dividing it into words calmed him. The money had not changed, but the hand choosing his next move became slower.

choices.text: Have to go bigger — this is the moment
choices.result_text:
If he missed this momentum, the same chance might never return. {name} checked his limit and entered an order larger than usual.

He had not pressed Confirm, yet his heart beat like it already knew the result. Bigger. Just once more. He erased the amount and typed it again. The sentence remained brighter in his mind than the screen.

choices.text: Decided not to tell anyone
choices.result_text:
{name} decided to tell no one. If his family knew, the number would become an expectation. If friends knew, it would require an explanation. For now, he wanted the money alone on his side.

He placed the phone face down. Only he knew the balance in this room. The secret was smaller than the money but somehow heavier. An achievement no one had congratulated cooled on the goshiwon desk.

title: One Business Card
description:
The night before the confrontation.

Searching a pocket, {name} felt it catch on a finger.
His business card. The one he handed over the first day.
A private number written on the back by hand.

'I don't give this to people. This is only for you, Minjun.'

{name} turned the card over.
Same handwriting. Same person. A different story.

choices.text: Keep the card and meet him tomorrow
choices.result_text:
Did not throw it away.
Somewhere between knowing and pretending not to know,
{name} slipped the card back into the pocket.

choices.text: Put the card in a drawer. Did not want to carry it
choices.result_text:
The drawer closed.
{name} decided to go tomorrow with nothing in hand.

title: The Photo From That Night
description:
Night.

{name} took out the phone and opened the gallery.

One photo.
In front of a pojangmacha. The two of them together.
Jaehyuk had an arm around {name}'s shoulder and was smiling.

That night had been real.
Even if he was a con man, at least that smile that night — must have been real.

Or had even that been practiced?

choices.text: Decide to believe it was real
choices.result_text:
Did not delete it.
Outside the evidence folder, {name} simply left it there.
That night was that night.

choices.text: Delete the photo
choices.result_text:
Permanently deleted.
{name} turned the phone face down.

title: Someone You Can Call
description:
There was nothing in your hand.

{name} scrolled up and down the contact list.
Someone you could call.
More precisely — someone you could call in this state.

Hyunsu's name was there.

That business card. One photo of him in a suit after four years of exam prep.
'It's thanks to you, hyung.' That sentence.

choices.text: Call him
choices.result_text:
"Hyung, is something wrong?"

You did not say much. Just talked. Said things had been hard lately.
Hyunsu did not say much either. He just listened.

After hanging up, something felt a little different.

choices.text: Put the phone down
choices.result_text:
Could not do it.
For now, it felt like this had to be handled alone.
